title: The ML workflow from start to finish
intro: The eight steps of an ML project, under- and overfitting shown interactively, and the fit–predict–score trio that is identical across scikit-learn.
keyPoints: The eight steps: question → data → split → prepare features → pick model → fit → evaluate → tune.
The scikit-learn trio: fit() trains, predict() predicts, score() evaluates.
Underfitting = too simple (bad everywhere); overfitting = memorising (great train score, poor test score).
Always start with a simple baseline before trying more complex models.

sections.title: The eight steps at a glance

blocks.html: An ML project is a loop, not a straight line: evaluation almost always sends you back to an earlier step. The pitfall column matters as much as the steps.

blocks.html: Poor score? Pick different features, a different model or better data. Most time goes to data and features, not exotic models.

sections.title: Under- and overfitting in one picture

blocks.html: Underfitting: too simple, poor on train and test. Overfitting: too complex, memorizes the training data, poor test score. The sweet spot lies in between.
In the plot: training error always drops, test error drops first and then rises — that is where overfitting starts. Play with the sliders.

blocks.title: Train and test error against model complexity
blocks.subtitle: The U-shape of the test error is the hallmark of overfitting. Drag the sliders — the live metrics track the lowest test error and the gap between train and test error on the right.

rows: more complex model, more or better features

blocks.html: Diagnosis: small train/test gap = healthy; large gap = overfitting; both poor = underfitting.
Every model has the same three methods: fit(X_train, y_train) trains, predict(X) predicts, score(X_test, y_test) evaluates — whether you pick KNN, LogisticRegression or an SVM.

blocks.caption: the trio in action
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1], [3, 12, 2], [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3], [9, 30, 2], [2,  9, 1],
              [6, 20, 3], [8, 26, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4, 15, 8, 5], dtype=float)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)                      # 1) learn
print('coefficients   :', model.coef_.round(2))
print('intercept      :', model.intercept_.round(2))
print('predictions    :', model.predict(X_test).round(1))          # 2) apply
print('test score (R2):', model.score(X_test, y_test).round(2))    # 3) judge

blocks.html: What fit yields are the coefficients: the rules the model learned. How they are trained is covered in chapters 2–4.

Checklist before you start coding:

  • Can I formulate my question as a prediction (number or category)?
  • Do I have data that actually contains the answer — and enough rows?
  • Do I know how I will measure success (which metric, which threshold)?
  • Have I split train and test data before anything else?
  • Am I starting with a simple model as a baseline?
Further reading: scikit-learn (ch1), math & loss (ch2), logistic regression (ch3), SVMs (ch4), trees (ch5), calculus (ch6), evaluation (ch7).
